source: Shapin and Schaffer (1985) Leviathan and the Air-Pump (read via Wikipedia article, secondary)
finding: Boyle-Hobbes dispute over the air-pump as a case of how experimental facts gain credibility. Facts rest on a material technology (the pump), a literary technology (reports that let absent readers 'witness') and a social technology (rules for how experimenters treat each other). The choice of method was also a choice of social order after 1660.
numbers: Book 1985, Princeton UP, 440 pages; 2nd ed 2011. Key experiments: Torricellian tube in the receiver; adhering marble/glass discs. Wikipedia gives no mercury heights.
limits: Wikipedia summary, not the book. Critics: Principe (presentist reading of Boyle), Horstmann (factual errors in the Hobbes chapters), Malcolm and Leijenhorst (Hobbes's anti-void view had no political motive), Latour (nature also shapes politics).
agent_relevance: Background: facts are credible when procedures are public, witnessed and checkable. Supports G2/G3. Do not adopt the claim that credibility is only social.

source: Shapin and Schaffer (1985): the leaking pump and Huygens's anomalous suspension (read via Wikipedia)
finding: The pump leaked, and the authors argue leakage was central: failures could be blamed on leaks, so the pump alone could not settle disputes. Huygens built his own pump and saw water stay suspended in an evacuated tube; Boyle's group could not reproduce it for over 18 months until Huygens came to London.
numbers: Over 18 months of failed replication; accepted only after the originator showed it on site.
limits: Wikipedia summary; Principe and others dispute details.
agent_relevance: Replication can depend on tacit skill and the original hardware. A failed re-run of a check is not a refutation until the check itself is validated (see a12).

source: Wikipedia: Robert Boyle (air-pump and Boyle's law facts)
finding: Boyle read of von Guericke's pump in 1657 and with Robert Hooke built an improved 'Pneumatical Engine' by 1659. His 1660 book New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall reported results. Boyle's law was first stated while answering the Jesuit Francis Line; Henry Power formulated the hypothesis in 1661.
numbers: Receiver 28.4 litres, 36 cm brass pumping cylinder; Guericke's design needed two strong men for hours; Boyle's law 1662; Mariotte 1676; Boyle elected Fellow 1663.
limits: Encyclopedia summary. No pressure-volume tables given.
agent_relevance: Hooke, a paid instrument-maker, did much of the hands-on work: hidden technicians are part of how facts are made. In our agent the code runner plays this role.

source: Wikipedia: Royal Society (founding facts)
finding: The Society started on 28 Nov 1660 when 12 natural philosophers at Gresham College decided to found a college for experimental learning. Motto 'Nullius in verba'. Philosophical Transactions began 1665 under Henry Oldenburg, the first journal devoted only to science. Hooke became Curator of Experiments Nov 1663.
numbers: First charter 15 July 1662 (Brouncker first president); second charter 22/23 April 1663; 98 original Fellows (94 on 20 May, 4 on 22 June 1663).
limits: The page is inconsistent on the second charter date (22 vs 23 April).
agent_relevance: Institutional form: a registry of dated, attributed claims plus witnesses. Maps to the agent's ledger of claims and checks.

source: Wikipedia: Micrographia (Hooke 1665)
finding: Hooke's illustrated microscope book was the Royal Society's first major publication and its first scientific best-seller. It coined the word 'cell' for cork. The louse engraving folds out to four times the book's size. Specimens needed heavy preparation to be visible.
numbers: Published Jan 1665 by Martyn and Allestry. Pepys: 'the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life'.
quote: the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life
limits: Wikipedia gives no count of observations. The 'instruments as prosthetic senses' claim is not covered by the page.
agent_relevance: Pictures act as portable witnesses. For an LLM agent: attach the raw output to a claim, not only a description.

source: Wikipedia: Sidereus Nuncius (Galileo 1610)
finding: Galileo's 20x telescope showed 4 moons of Jupiter, lunar mountains and many more stars. Few others could see the moons at first because good telescopes were scarce; optics of the day could not show the instrument was not deceiving the senses. Court-sent spyglasses spread the instrument.
numbers: Published 13 Mar 1610; first saw Jupiter's moons 7 Jan 1610 (Gregorian); 35 stars in the Pleiades vs 6 naked eye; 80 in Orion vs 9; mountains 'at least four miles high'; early telescopes 8-10x; Kepler endorsed in Apr 1610 but had no independent confirmation until Aug 1610.
limits: Wikipedia summary; no print-run figure.
agent_relevance: New instrument, trust problem: a result is believed when others get the same observation with their own copies. Supports G3/G4: independent reproduction, not one source repeated.

source: Wikipedia: Christiaan Huygens (air-pump link)
finding: Huygens learned of Boyle's pump work at Gresham College in 1661, then tested a new hypothesis with his own experiments. He became the Royal Society's first foreign Fellow in 1663.
numbers: Visit 1661; Fellow 1663; pendulum clock invented and patented 1657.
limits: Only the first 100k of 311k characters were read; anomalous suspension was not in that part.
agent_relevance: Foreign replication: independent labs with different hardware are the strongest check. Parallel: a different model or tool, not a resample of the same one.

source: Merton thesis (Wikipedia summary of Merton 1936/1938, Science, Technology and Society in Seventeenth-Century England)
finding: Merton argued Puritan and Pietist values fed the rise of English science and the Royal Society. Critics: neglects mathematics and the mechanical philosophy; cannot define the 'right type' of Protestant; cannot explain Catholic scientists (Copernicus, Descartes, Galileo). Merton replied that Puritanism helped but was not necessary.
numbers: Dissertation 1936; monograph 1938; Lenski 1958/1963 Detroit study found Catholics less drawn to science careers. Wikipedia gives no Royal Society percentages.
limits: No DNB counts on the page. Quantitative support is disputed; see Cohen (ed) 1990 and Shapin 1988 (not opened).
agent_relevance: Background only. A correlation between a group trait and success needs the counterexamples checked (G3).

source: Merton (1942) 'Science and Technology in a Democratic Order': the four norms (read via Wikipedia, Mertonian norms)
finding: Four institutional imperatives of science: communism (knowledge is common property), universalism (judge claims by impersonal criteria), disinterestedness, organized skepticism. Merton said peer scrutiny explains the low rate of fraud.
numbers: Mitroff 1974 (Apollo moon scientists, ASR vol 39 no 4) proposed counter-norms: secrecy, particularism, self-interestedness, organized dogmatism. Later acronym CUDOS adds Originality; Ziman 2000; Anderson et al 2010.
limits: Page has no empirical test numbers and carries a missing-citations tag.
agent_relevance: Maps onto the schema: universalism = judge a claim by the check, not by who or which model said it; organized skepticism = doubt only on a signal (G1).

source: Wikipedia: Boris Hessen (1931 Newton talk)
finding: At the 1931 London congress Hessen argued the Principia answered technical and economic needs of the 17th century, with ballistics central. This opened externalist history of science; critics call it 'vulgar Marxism'.
numbers: Talk 1931; arrested 22 Aug 1936; shot 20 Dec 1936; rehabilitated 1956.
limits: Strong economic determinism not accepted by most Western historians.
agent_relevance: Background only: the 'external pressure' view. Little direct use for the scaffold.

source: Wikipedia: Laboratory Life (Latour and Woolgar 1979)
finding: Ethnography of Guillemin's Salk lab: the lab works as an inscription factory; the main output is papers. Statements move along a five-level facticity scale. TRF(H) narrowed the field to structure determination, raising the entry cost for rivals. Careers run on a cycle of credibility.
numbers: 1979 first edition; 1986 edition dropped 'social' from the subtitle.
limits: Secondary summary; later reframed as actor-network theory.
agent_relevance: The facticity scale is close to our status marks [E]/[S]/[D]: statements rise in status as qualifiers are stripped by checks.

source: Wikipedia: Experimenter's regress (Collins 1985, Changing Order)
finding: Collins: you need a good experiment to test a theory and a correct result to know the experiment is good, so replication alone cannot settle a dispute; it is ended by social negotiation. Extended to the theoretician's regress (Kennefick 2000) and simulationist's regress (Gelfert 2011).
numbers: Weber's gravity-wave claims were answered technically but not accepted. No numbers on the page.
limits: TEA-laser example and Franklin's critique are not on the page.
agent_relevance: When checker and claim disagree, add an independent anchor (held-out test, symmetry) rather than more of the same check (G3).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? arXiv:2409.04109 (full text read)
finding: Blind expert review of human ideas against LLM ideas. LLM ideas were judged more novel (p<0.05) and slightly less feasible (n.s.). Human reranking of LLM ideas widened the gap.
numbers: N=49 idea writers, N=79 reviewers (104 distinct people), 298 reviews. Review-level novelty: human 4.84 (n=119) vs AI 5.64 (n=109), Bonferroni p<0.01; AI excitement 5.19 p=0.04 vs human; feasibility human 6.61 vs AI 6.34 (p=1.00). Idea-level excitement: human 4.56, AI 5.18 (p=0.08), AI+rerank 5.45 (p<0.01).
limits: Ideas not executed. Inter-reviewer agreement only 56.1% vs 66.0% (NeurIPS 2021) and 71.9% (ICLR 2024).
agent_relevance: The institution here is blind review. Novelty is judged by a panel, not tested by experiment, so it is weak evidence of truth.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024): generation limits (duplicates, LLM judge)
finding: Scaling LLM idea generation gives mostly duplicates, and LLM-as-judge is not a reliable evaluator of ideas.
numbers: About 5% of seed ideas remained after deduplication at cosine similarity 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2); the best LLM ranker reached 71.4% accuracy (Claude-3.5-Sonnet) vs 61-64% for others on the pairwise decision task.
limits: NLP prompting ideas only; one pipeline.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model are not independent (G4). Diversity must come from different sources, like labs with different pumps.

source: Lu et al (2024) The AI Scientist, arXiv:2408.06292 (full text read)
finding: End-to-end pipeline: idea, code, experiments, paper, then an automated reviewer. Claude 3.5 Sonnet gave the best papers; the authors list hallucinated results and weak experiments.
numbers: About $10-15 per paper; reviewer $0.25-0.50 per review; Weak Accept = score 6.
limits: Reviewer cannot ask questions; hallucinated plots and ablation tables seen; GPT-4o often failed on LaTeX; DeepSeek Coder failed tool calls.
agent_relevance: The pipeline copies the institution (journal and referee) around the lab. Without real instruments it hallucinates results: G2 matters.

source: Lu et al (2024) AI Scientist automated reviewer accuracy
finding: The LLM reviewer matches humans on balanced accuracy but with different error types: fewer false negatives, more false positives.
numbers: Balanced accuracy 0.65 vs human 0.66; F1 0.57 vs 0.49; AUC 0.65 vs 0.65; FNR 0.39 vs 0.52; FPR 0.31 vs 0.17. On the imbalanced ICLR 2022 set accuracy is below the human 73%.
limits: OpenReview data; the model may have seen the papers; class imbalance affects accuracy.
agent_relevance: Peer review is a noisy social instrument; even human referees are only about 66% consistent, so one reviewer is not truth.

source: Jin et al (2024) AgentReview: peer review dynamics with LLM agents, arXiv:2406.12708 (full text read)
finding: LLM agents simulate reviewers, authors and area chairs. Conformity: rating spread falls 27.2% after the reviewer-AC discussion. One under-committed reviewer cut others' review length 18.7% (195.5 to 159.0 words).
numbers: Over 53,800 generated documents, 10,000+ reviews, 500+ ICLR submissions 2020-2023; acceptance fixed at 32%; sample 350 rejected, 125 posters, 29 spotlights, 19 orals.
limits: No direct comparison with real review outcomes; interactions among factors not modelled.
agent_relevance: Social influence among LLM agents is real: discussion makes agents converge, a risk for any multi-agent check (G4).

source: Jin et al: bias and authority effects (AgentReview)
finding: Telling reviewers an author is renowned changes outcomes, more for lower-quality papers and more with more reviewers informed. Rebuttal removal changed little (anchoring).
numbers: 37.1% of decisions varied with reviewer bias; 27.7% decision change when all reviewers know identities for 10% of papers; Jaccard 0.364, 0.154, 0.008 for 1, 2, 3 informed reviewers; 'lack of novelty' in 10.4% of malicious comments vs 3.69% benign (+182.9%).
limits: Simulation, not human data. LLM reviews share at least 2/3/4 of 4 points with human reviews in 90%/77%/39% of 100 papers.
agent_relevance: Universalism can be tested on agents: blind the source. Our schema strips model identity from checks.

source: Schmidgall et al (2025) Agent Laboratory, arXiv:2501.04227 (read)
finding: Human-in-the-loop research pipeline. The automated NeurIPS-style reviewer overestimates quality compared to human reviewers.
numbers: Automated overall 6.1/10 vs human 3.8/10 (-2.3); autonomous papers 3.8, co-pilot 4.13 (+0.33); external reviewers 4.38 vs self 4.13; o1-preview most useful, o1-mini best experimental quality, gpt-4o behind.
limits: Small study; self-selected researcher samples.
agent_relevance: LLM referees are lenient. Keep a human or code anchor.

source: Schmidgall and Moor (2025) AgentRxiv, arXiv:2503.18102 (abstract read)
finding: Shared preprint server for agent labs. Agents with access to earlier reports improved more than isolated agents; several labs sharing progressed faster.
numbers: MATH-500 relative gain 11.4% (one lab with memory), 13.7% (several labs sharing); best method +3.3% average on other benchmarks.
limits: Abstract only; one benchmark family; contamination possible.
agent_relevance: Direct test of 'institution as memory': a shared ledger of earlier results helps. Candidate for our ledger design.

source: Gottweis et al (2025) Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist, arXiv:2502.18864 (abstract)
finding: Multi-agent Gemini system with generate-critique-refine and a tournament that improves with test-time compute. Validated on drug repurposing for AML and other biomedical tasks.
numbers: Quality gains with more compute; in-vitro validation for AML candidates; no figures in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; validation by the authors.
agent_relevance: Tournament of ideas plus a real lab check mimics institution plus instrument.

source: Algaba et al (2024) LLMs reflect human citation patterns with heightened citation bias, arXiv:2405.15739 (abstract)
finding: GPT-4, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 suggest references with a stronger bias to highly cited works than human authors, after controlling for year, title length, authors and venue.
numbers: Papers from AAAI, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR after the models' cutoff; no figures in the abstract.
limits: Parametric knowledge only, no search.
agent_relevance: LLMs amplify the Matthew effect. An agent that ranks sources by fame inherits the bias; weigh by check.

source: Shapin and Schaffer: social technology of the witness (from memory, not opened)
finding: Recalled: gentlemen's testimony counted most; Boyle reported trials, including failures, in circumstantial detail so readers could picture them.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: A log that records failed trials in detail increases checkability. Mirrors G2.

source: Shapin (1994) A Social History of Truth (not opened)
finding: Recalled: in 17th-century England trust in testimony was bound to gentlemanly status.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Contrast: source trust for the agent must come from checks, not status.

source: Collins (1985) Changing Order (not opened)
finding: Recalled: case studies of replication show no neutral criterion tells whether a replication succeeded.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened; a12 is the page that was read.
agent_relevance: Use two kinds of check, not one more copy.

source: Schaffer (1989) Glass works: Newton's prisms and the uses of experiment (not opened)
finding: Recalled: others could not reproduce Newton's prism results with their own prisms, so results travel only with matched instruments.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Record which tool and version made each check.
